# `sketchSky()` {#fn-sketchsky}

W02 verified the reconstructed Gacrux bearing and altitude at the same instant and viewpoint using direct equatorial coordinates and spherical geometry. [W02 results](w02-field-to-sky.qmd).

[Function index](function-index.html#idx-sketchsky)

```{=html}
<p>The function computes an object without drawing. Use
<code>plot(hor, sky = sky, xrange = ..., yrange = ...)</code> to choose the sector.
Replotting the object changes framing without recalculating the instant. Use
<code>skyStep</code> to recalculate at another time. Astronomical calculations
require Swiss Ephemeris files covering the epoch; see
<code>skyscapeR-package</code> for installation.
</p>
```

**Interpretation and limits.** For photometric claims work with the linear component matrices and pixel area. Changing the field of view or display mapping can change screen intensity even when integrated source flux is conserved.


<details><summary>Implementation arguments, return value and documented modes</summary>

```{=html}
<table><thead><tr><th>Argument</th><th>Formal default</th><th>Behaviour in this interface</th></tr></thead><tbody><tr><th scope="row"><code>hor</code></th><td>—</td><td><p>A <code>skyscapeR.horizon</code> with finite latitude, longitude and observer
elevation in metres in <code>metadata$georef</code>. The numerical profile supplies the
foreground when plotted. A panorama image is optional.</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>jd</code></th><td><code>NULL</code></td><td><p>One finite UT Julian day. Supply exactly one of <code>jd</code> and <code>time</code>.</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>time</code></th><td><code>NULL</code></td><td><p>A civil timestamp accepted by <code>time2jd</code>, or a POSIXt instant.</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>timezone</code></th><td>—</td><td><p>Civil timezone and calendar for character <code>time</code>, as
in <code>time2jd</code>. Defaults are the session settings. A POSIXt value already
identifies an instant; these arguments do not reinterpret it. Use UTC or a fixed
offset for ancient civil dates.</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>calendar</code></th><td>—</td><td><p>Civil timezone and calendar for character <code>time</code>, as
in <code>time2jd</code>. Defaults are the session settings. A POSIXt value already
identifies an instant; these arguments do not reinterpret it. Use UTC or a fixed
offset for ancient civil dates.</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>display</code></th><td><code>list()</code></td><td><p>A named list of logical switches: <code>sun</code>, <code>moon</code>,
<code>planets</code>, <code>stars</code>, <code>constellation.lines</code>, <code>milky.way</code>,
<code>galactic.equator</code>, <code>ecliptic</code>, <code>equator</code>, <code>poles</code> and
<code>zenith</code>. Sun, Moon and stars default to TRUE; other switches default to
FALSE, except that the Milky Way follows <code>stars</code> unless explicitly set.
The additional <code>constellations</code> entry accepts names or an imported data
frame, rather than a logical value. See Constellations below. A named logical
vector is sufficient when supplying only switches.</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>style</code></th><td><code>c(&quot;natural&quot;, &quot;publication-colour&quot;, &quot;publication-mono&quot;)</code></td><td><p>One of <code>"natural"</code>, <code>"publication-colour"</code> or
<code>"publication-mono"</code>. Publication styles have a white background and dark
guides. Colour uses muted stellar and planetary colours and a warm solar disc;
mono uses black and white. Neither publication style predicts visibility.</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>max.mag</code></th><td><code>6</code></td><td><p>Finite catalogue magnitude cutoff, default 6. Applied before
extinction to star symbols and the integrated magnitudes of supported clusters.
It does not limit constellation endpoints, the Sun, Moon or planets. Raising
the cutoff includes additional stars only where the catalogue supplies them.</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>k</code></th><td><code>skyscapeR.vars()$k</code></td><td><p>Non-negative visual extinction coefficient in magnitudes per airmass
for natural style. Defaults to <code>skyscapeR.vars()$k</code>, initially 0.2.
This clear-sky baseline is an assumption, not an estimate of the site's weather.
Zero removes extinction and the modelled lunar scattering. Publication styles
do not apply extinction to symbols.</p></td></tr></tbody></table><h5>Return value</h5><p>An object of classes <code>skyscapeR.sketch</code> and <code>skyscapeR.sky</code>.
It stores <code>jd</code>, <code>loc</code>, <code>style</code>, <code>display</code>, <code>settings</code>
(calendar, magnitude cutoff and extinction), and <code>atmosphere</code>.
<code>stars</code> and <code>coords</code> contain azimuth, altitude and symbol size;
<code>star.opacity</code> retains an earlier symbol-opacity diagnostic; natural
sketches draw from <code>light.budget</code>. <code>bodies</code>, <code>diameters</code>,
<code>planet.size</code> and <code>lunar</code> describe selected Solar System bodies.
<code>clusters</code> holds supported cluster footprints and opacity when applicable;
<code>guides</code>, <code>light</code>, <code>background</code> and twilight fields support drawing.
Components can be empty when a layer is disabled. No image file is written.
</p><h5>Reading a natural sketch</h5><p>The sky is calculated for the specified instant. Stars, clusters, planets and
the Moon contribute light on a common visual (V-band) magnitude scale.
Diffuse Milky Way light and atmospheric background are measured per unit
sky area. Their light is added before brightness is compressed for display.
To inspect the values underlying a view, use <code>skyRadiance</code>.
</p><p>Stars remain unresolved as the field is enlarged. Mercury, Venus, Mars,
Jupiter, Saturn and the Moon use apparent disc sizes and illuminated
fractions from Swiss Ephemeris. A close view can therefore show the phase
of Venus. Star colours follow catalogue spectral classes; the diffuse band
has a neutral tint. Colour and projection influence the screen appearance.
Publication styles use magnitude-scaled star and planet symbols on white.
</p><p>Azimuth increases clockwise from true north. Refraction, pressure and
temperature come from <code>skyscapeR.vars</code> when the sky is calculated.
The Sun and Moon switches control their contributions to sky illumination as
well as their discs. Use <code>display = list(moon = FALSE)</code> for a moonless
comparison. The terrain masks the drawn sky; a local ridge hiding the Moon
can still leave scattered moonlight in the sky.
</p><h5>Constellations</h5><p>Use <code>display = list(constellations = "Orion")</code> to select and enable line
figures. <code>"modern"</code> selects all 88 Western figures, <code>"chinese"</code> the
full Chinese set, and <code>"chinese_mansions"</code> the 28 lunar-mansion figures.
Names and abbreviations are case-sensitive; for example <code>c("Ori", "Tau")</code>.
Alternatively, supply a data frame from <code>importConstellations</code>.
See <code>constellations</code> for sources and identifiers.
</p><p>Supplying a selection enables lines unless <code>constellation.lines = FALSE</code>
is also supplied. Setting <code>constellation.lines = TRUE</code> without a selection
uses modern figures. Endpoint coordinates are calculated independently of the
star-symbol magnitude cut. Lines therefore remain when their stars are faint,
extincted, or switched off. A single-star figure is drawn as a ring. Normal
plot clipping and the horizon foreground still apply. These are reference
figures; their visibility is not an observing prediction.
</p><h5>Twilight and extinction</h5><p>At twilight the sky brightens differently towards and away from the Sun.
Zenith brightness uses the Paranal V-band observations of Patat et al.
(2006) at solar depressions of 5 to 15 degrees. Sacramento Peak measurements
supply earlier twilight levels and the directional variation (Koomen et al.
1952). These clear-sky estimates depend on site conditions. Moonlight uses
the scattering model of Krisciunas and Schaefer (1991), with its dependence
on lunar phase, altitude and angular separation.
</p><p>Direct light fades towards the horizon as its path through the atmosphere
lengthens. The coefficient <code>k</code> sets the loss per airmass. The model
uses Rozenberg's airmass approximation (Krisciunas and Schaefer 1991);
uncertainty is greatest close to the skyline. The twilight colours are
illustrative (Lee 1994, 2015).
</p><h5>Milky Way and clusters</h5><p>The Milky Way is traced from the diffuse light in Deep Star Maps 2020.
Within the smoothed envelope, retained dark patches have at least 10 percent
local contrast; two bright tiers begin at 1.10 and 1.75 times the mean band
tone after the dark patches are excluded. Retained patches cover at least
10 square degrees. Natural sketches anchor the mean surface brightness
of a four-degree field in Carina to 20.7 V magnitudes per square arcsecond
(van der Kruit 2024). Brightness elsewhere is approximate. Atmospheric
extinction can make the band difficult to follow down to its calculated
horizon crossing. The Galactic equator is an optional geometric guide.
</p><p>A supported cluster contributes its catalogue light across its angular
extent. Light already assigned to plotted stars within that footprint is
subtracted before the remaining glow is drawn. This accounts for projected
overlap; it does not establish membership. Integrated cluster magnitude
alone is insufficient to predict first detection (Crumey 2014).
</p><h5>Using a sketch with a stellar phase date</h5><p>In 69 of 70 individual comparisons, the estimated first morning of visibility was within a week of the predicted heliacal-rising date.
</p><p>Use <code>riseset</code> to locate the skyline crossing on each morning,
then <code>skyStep</code> to follow the star as it climbs through a
brightening sky. A plotted pixel does not establish naked-eye visibility.
A quantitative test needs a point-source threshold and an assumed observer
limit (Crumey 2014). See also <code>star.phases</code>.
Record site, horizon, epoch, calendar, timezone, extinction
and display switches when reporting a reconstruction.
</p>
```

</details>
